meta.description:
Delivers critical electrical support for the DoW’s largest Joint Base
encompassing 4.1K facilities & a $50B infrastructure. Maintains 2 airfield lighting systems supporting 40 C-17s & 132 helicopters valued at $121B. Ensures strict compliance with safety regulations (Unified Facilities Criteria, National Electric Code & Army Corps of Engineers) & upkeeps a $495K emergency airfield lighting system.

meta.jhaNotes:
Material Handling: Always lift with your legs, not your back. Squat down, grasp the item close to your body, and lift straight up. Do not twist your body to turn. If you need to turn, pivor on your heels in the direction you need to turn. Avoid any necessary twisting and lower the item in the same way you lift it. If you need help lifting an object because it is too heavy or awkward, ask for assistance

Walking/Working Surfaces: Walk, don't run. Be aware of items (cords, loose carpet, pencils, paper, ETC...) that may cause you to slip/trip and fall. Climb stairs facing forward, stay to the right side, use the handrail and avoid distractions that may cause you to fall. Do not run up or down stairs. 

Stairwell Safety: Do not run up or down stairs, always use hand rails. Do not skip steps if in a hurry. If carrying packages, be sure of your footing. When climbing stairs stay to your right. When going down stairs stay to your right. Report any damage to stairs or hand rails to building manager. 

Electrical Hazards: Computers and other electrically powered equipment are used in the office environment. Ensure all electrically operated equipment has a ground progn, if manufactured with one, and that all prongs are securely attached. When plugging and unplugging electrical equipment, grasp the base of the cord. Frequently inspect cords for damage. If you feel a shock or tingling sensation when touching a piece of equipment, turn it off at the power strip or circuit breaker and notify your supervisor. Multiple plug adapters will not be used solely as wiring to provide additional or more convenient outlets. Power strips should only support low wattage equipment. Do not plug in coffee makers, microwaves, refrigerators, etc. into theres. In additon, do not plug any higher amperage devices into modular furniture (microwaves, toasters, refrigerators), as the wiring inside is not designed to carry these loads and a fire may result. 

Hand Tool Safety: You may occasionally be required to use tools in the office. Ensure you always cut away from your body. Do not carry and/or store unguarded blades or sharp object in your pockets or desk drawers. here are assortments of hand tools that may be used in an office environment. Ensure that all tools are used for the purposes for which they were designed. Inspect tools prior to use. If an unsafe tool is found, remove it from service and report it to your supervisor. 

Repetitive Motion Hazard: Repetitive tasks such as typing may create problems for some individusals. To avoid such problems, alternate tasks to prevent your over-exertion of a particular body part or series of parts. Your supervisor should provide ou with the latitude to alternate tasks without hindering mission effectiveness. Schedule your daily tasks with this in mind. 

Office Safety: Desks, tables, and many other pieces of office furniture have sharp corners that can cause injury. Use caution particularly when walking around desks. Open file cabinet drawers one at a time to prevent possible tipping. Desk and cabinet drawers should never be left unattended in the open position. Position office equipment in a manner that egress and ease of movement is not hampered. Proper sitting is important. Employees leaning back or sitting on the front edge of the seat creates mishaps/falls from chairs. 

Flight Line Hazards: Do not operate any vehcile on the flight line unless you have received flight line driver training and are in possession of a current AF Form 483. The flight line is a designated Hazardous Noise Area. Always carry appropriate hearing protection with you and wear it. Stay clear of RF radiation hazard areas, which are condoned off by Avionics personnel during radar tests. 

Working with High Voltage Distribution System up to 13.8 KV: (Live-line maintenance is strictly prohibited as outlined in AFI 32-1064.) The only provision to this is when authorized by the JBLM Commander or equivalent to support a critical mission, prevent injury to persons, or protect property.  Further guidance is available in AFI 32-1064.

Working on energized and deenergized circuits (LOTO 29CFR 190.147, AFOSH Std. 91-501) : When working on energized or de-energized circuits, all circuits must be treated as if they were live. Lockout & Tagout/Safe Clearance 269 must be used at all times

Working at heights above 4 feet (Fall Protection) (29CFR 190.66, AFOSH Std. 91-501):Ensure all ladders utilized are made of fiberglass and are in serviceable condition. When working from high-reach vehicles or aerial platforms, hard hats and body harnesses will be utilized with no exceptions.

Working with or around Hazardous Substances: (HAZCOM 29CFR 1910. 1200, AFI 90-821) Hazardous substance can be found in transformers and switchgears which are called PCB's. Chemicals you may work with or are exposed to can be harmful. Most substances are located in our MSDS binder and must be on AUL. Know who your Environmental Control Officer is. HAZCOM and Asbestos awareness training are to be completed annually and annotated in AF Form 55.

Working with hazards within the work area of the Active Flight-line: When working around air dome, personnel must be aware of surroundings at all times for aircraft and vehicles. When working on airfield circuits, all circuits must be de-energized prior to work. When working on airfield workers must be in contact with McChord Ground at all times. Drivers must have a valid airfield license to operate vehicles on flight-line.

Flight-line Driving: All personnel will be qualified and permitted before operating vehicles and (or) equipment on the flight-line.  Upon completion of training, issue of AF Form 483, Certificate of Competency, endorsed for flight-line driving.

Working with Confined Spaces and oxygen deficient areas: (29CFR 1910.146, DAFMAN 91-203 Confined Spaces program.) Confined spaces are defined as an enclosed area with one way in and one way out, such as manholes. Consider all manholes to be permit required until proper testing and monitoring has been accomplished. No one will enter manholes without the proper permit clearance.

Working on or around hazardous noise areas: (29CFR 1910.95, & AFOSH STD 48-20) Upon assigned to shop, personnel must report to Environmental Health for proper fitting of ear plugs. Supervisor must insure personnel have annual audiogram at Occupational Health Medical Examination. When working around machinery or loud noise personnel must wear earplugs/muff/ear defenders. 

Asbestos Awareness:Shop personnel will be trained on asbestos awareness. OSHA Class IV Asbestos Training Safety OJT. They will know how to identify the hazards of asbestos and how report it. Training is documented in AF Form 55.

Electrical Cleaning Operations: Cleaning of electrical contacts and other electrical components is normally done with contacts cleaners. These cleaners are normally sprayed on and remove dirt grease and oil condensation.  Manual application and wiping with dry cloth can also be accomplished. In addition dry/air cleaning and vacuuming afterwards is also common in tight and sensitive areas. 

Electrical Sealing and Bonding: Electrical repair maintenance tasking requires the use of adhesives, glues and other bonding agents to adhere or join electrical parts and components.  Also includes sealant and caulk used to seal or cover and close cracks, gaps, and openings.  This activity is only geared towards electrical systems maintenance and repairs. 

Disassembly and Inspection: This includes visual inspection, removal and installation of minor or major components, parts, hardware... etc. It can be part of maintenance or repair, accomplished in order to replace a malfunctioning or worn part or as part of a preventative maintenance requirement.  It could be accomplished in less controlled environments which might expose personnel to hazardous noise, confined spaces, explosive atmospheres, and larger quantities of pools or other chemicals.  It may also require the handling of objects and fixtures that are heavy. 

Manual and Powered Hoist: Operator training and extensive workplace precautions will be developed and used when moving large, heavy loads.  Safety issues considering both the operator and worker while usage of such diverse "lifting" devices when in proximity to them.  See shop lesson plan, manufacture training material or State specific lesson plans.

Wearing Jewelry in Workplace: Wearing jewelry (finger rings/necklace) should be restricted.  WARNING: Placing tape over rings or wearing gloves on the hand with a ring does not provide protection or eliminate this requirement. Must protect yourself from electrical shock at all times.

Portable and Fixed Ladder Safety: Safe use of ladders requires proper climbing practices at all times.  Ensure to check for ladder defects and slippery substances, wear slip-resistant shoes with heels, never jump from ladder, and remove hand jewelry prior to climbing. Do not stand on top step of any ladder.

Walking/Working Surfaces: Tripping hazards, water or other material on the floor often cause employees to trip/slip and fall.  Maintain alertness while walking. Beware of loading dock edges.  Practice good situational awareness.

Housekeeping: Ensure your work area is kept neat and clean at all times.  Do not store excessive amounts of combustibles in an office environment. Clean up spills as soon as they occur.  Good housekeeping practices reduce the possibility of fires and injuries.  Dispose of perishable food as needed.

Controlled Access Areas: Do not attempt to enter controlled access areas without proper clearance.

Designated Smoking Areas: No smoking is allowed inside any building on base.  Smoking is permitted only in designated Tobacco Use Areas.  The smoking area for this building is located next to the outside shed on the north side of the building.
meta.medicalFacility:
Madigan Army Medical Center is located on Lewis Main and is on Jackson Ave. The emergency room is located on the north side of the building. All active duty military personnel, whether full-time or part-time, are authorized to use the hospital for emergency treatment. 

For non-emergencies, appointments must be made at McChord medical appointment line, phone number: 1-800-404-4506.  Dental services are also available at McChord by calling 982-5505.  Call 911 for emergencies.

Air Force and DoD civilian personnel must complete a Form CA-1 or CA-6 (obtained from supervisor/safety representative).  This should be completed as soon as possible after medical treatment is sought.  Contact the civilian personnel office for assistance.
meta.evacuationRoute:
Evacuation Procedures: Upon notification, evacuate the area/building immediately. Secure sensitive information (bring it with you if needed).  Do not lock doors, use the telephone, or operate any electronic equipment until you have arrived at the office assembly area.

Primary Assembly Point: In front of Bldg 555 (in the parking lot close to the Chaple Support Center). Alternate Assembly Point: Is located at Bldg. 588 (Parking lot).  NOTE: When exiting the building, if the Primary Assembly Point is downwind we'll automatically rally at the Alternate location.

There are two types of pull boxes currently in use.  One has a glass window with a black push button inside.  To activate the alarm, break the glass and push the button firmly. The second type has a clear plastic flap with a pull handle underneath.  To activate this type, lift the flap and pull the handle.

If fire extinguishers are available for employee use, it is the to educate employees on the principles and practices of using a fire extinguisher and the hazards associated with fighting small or developing fires. This education must be provided when a new employee is first hired, and annually thereafter.  Fire extinguisher training is located in ADLS.  Document on AF Form 55 (or equivalent).  



Small Fire: Call 911 immediately.  State the nature of the emergency.  Give your Bldg number, name, rank, and phone number.  You may attempt to fight these fires if you are properly trained and have the proper equipment (extinguisher). 

Large Fire: Call 911 immediately.  Activate fire alarm and evacuate the area. 
S: Sound the alarm 
P: Phone the Fire Department Dial 911 giving your name and location.  
E: Extinguish the fire if it is small and you are not in danger! 
E: Evacuate the Facility/Area. Calmly notify personnel to leave the scene. 
D: Direct Fire Personnel to the location of fire.
meta.safetyBoardLocation: The Safety Bulletin board is located in the hallway of bldg. 556 next to the Front Entrance.  You should review it periodically.  Pay particular attention to the guidelines set forth on AFVA 91-209, Air Force Occupational Safety and Health Program.  AFVA 91-209 is used to identify and provide contact information for your Safety Chain of Command and can be found on all Safety Boards.
meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
Mandatory use of seat belts:  Mishap experience has proven time after time that safety belts prevent injuries and save lives.  If you are involved in a vehicle mishap and you are not wearing your seatbelt, you stand five times greater chance of being thrown from the vehicle.  Additionally, your body acts as a projectile and could strike other passengers causing death and serious injury.   Also, as a vehicle operator, you are responsible for ensuring all passengers are using safety belts.  Traffic violations for passengers not wearing safety belts go to the operator.

Note:  Placing the shoulder strap under the arm or not using/disconnecting automatic belts constitutes improper use and may result in a citation or more seriously, death or disability.

IAW DODI 6055.4 (Traffic Safety Program) and AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, the use of headphones, earphones, and cellular telephones is prohibited while operating a vehicle on a DoD installation.  The only caveat to this is using a hands free device or in hands-free operating mode.  

AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, outlines the requirements for seat belt use.  Safety belts will be worn by anyone driving or riding in a vehicle on base.  Active duty personnel must wear safety belts when operating a vehicle (regardless whether it is a GOV or POV) on or off base.  AF civilian personnel on duty must wear seat belts on or off a DoD installation    Children 1.50 meters (4 ft, 9 inches) in height or smaller regardless of age must be in an infant seat or child restraint device.

Speed limits:
You as a driver have to follow speed limits on and off base. On base the general speed limit is 25 mph if no other sign is posted. The basic speed limit off base is 35 mph in built-up areas and 55 mph on roadways. Typically, on highways, it is 60 mph.  If you are hauling a trailer, camper, or boat, reduce your speed to prevent from tipping over or jackknifing.

Local traffic hazards:
Driving during winter in this area is extremely dangerous with ice and snow because the roads are over populated and there are numerous curves and hills.  Black ice can increase risk of accidents, so slow down and take your time during the winter months.  We would rather have you arrive a few minutes late, than not at all! 

Highway I-5:  You may or may not have heard of the motor vehicle mishaps on the I-5; however, according to the Air Force Safety Center, the Air Force loses roughly on average 18 Airmen annually due to fatal motor vehicle mishaps. Protect yourself by reducing your speed and driving defensively.  This means expect other drivers to speed and pass at the worst times, and adjust your driving to avoid an accident. 

Rural Roads:  Here in Washington, we have roadways 7, 8, 12, 101, 121, 161, 162, 167, 410, 507, 510, 512, and 706.  These roadways on average have a maximum speed limit of 35 mph to 60 mph.  These roadways can also become congested with traffic and occasional farm equipment.  If you are stuck behind a piece of farm equipment, do not try passing unless it is safe and legal to do so.  Be sure to plan ahead so you do not need to rush.  Lastly, during the wintertime, these roads are secondary when it comes to sanding and plowing.  It is important to know this in case you need to make other arrangements when it comes to getting to your destination.  The most serious accidents occur when people drive faster than the road conditions will safely allow.  Use common sense and reduce your speed for poor weather conditions and congested traffic.
meta.trafficContacts:
Motorcycle riders: Motorcycle riders must have a motorcycle endorsement from a state, and have attended a Motorcycle Safety Foundation (Basic Rider or Basic rider II Course).  Additionally, each rider must make contact with their unit Motorcycle Safety Representative (MSR).  The rider must receive a one-on-one brief from their commander or designated representative before riding.  This course is mandatory for all riders before they can ride.  All riders must also complete an MSF-approved intermediate training course (sport bike riders must take a sport bike riding course) ideally within 60 days but no later than one year after completing initial training. See AFI 91-207.  Annual preseason briefings are also required.

selectedModules.title: Hazardous Energy Control
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 21; 29 CFR 1910.147 - The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train authorized employees to recognize hazardous energy sources, the type and magnitude of energy present, and the methods and means for isolation and control. Train affected employees on the purpose and use of lockout/tagout procedures, and instruct all other employees on the prohibition against restarting locked or tagged equipment.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Document initial and refresher training when job assignments, machines, processes, or energy control procedures change, or when inspections show employee knowledge gaps.

selectedModules.title: Hazard Communication
selectedModules.reference: DAFI 90-821; 29 CFR 1910.1200 - Hazard Communication
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train personnel on hazardous chemicals in their work area, labeling systems, safety data sheets, and the measures they can take to protect themselves during normal operations and foreseeable emergencies.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide HazCom training upon initial assignment, whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced, and when new tasks expose workers to different hazardous materials. Ensure workers know how to access local SDS information and labeling guidance.
selectedModules.notes:
Reference: DPW OMD Safety Program, AFI 90-821, Hazard Communication, and 29 CFR 1910.1200.

Commanders must ensure supervisors and employees who handle, use, or are potentially exposed to hazardous materials/chemicals in the course of official AF duties are provided information and training on the AFHCP and the specific hazards in their work areas. 
Normally, employees working in administrative areas do not have exposures to hazardous materials/chemicals. However, there may be occasions when employees are exposed. Examples may be when they handle paints, adhesives, oils, petroleum products, etc. during minor "self-help" type construction/facility up-keep or other miscellaneous details. These individuals do not require HAZCOM training unless they are working with chemicals that require a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) or otherwise directed by Public Health or Bioenvironmental. 
Personnel require both Federal and Work center specific HAZCOM training. Training must be conducted upon initial work area assignment and whenever a new hazard is introduced into the work area. Initial training will occur before employees are exposed to hazardous materials. 
Supervisors must ensure training is documented on the AF Form 55, Employee Safety and Health Record. Documentation will be added in Section V of AF Form 55 as: "Federal Hazard Communication Training Program (FHCTP)" for the initial training and "Workplace Specific FHCTP" for each presentation of specific workplace hazard information. 
Workers should be familiar with locations of SDSs and have a basic knowledge of their use and information. 

Workplace Supervisors will: 
Maintain a Workplace Specific Hazard Communications binder with identified hazardous or controlled chemicals maintained and/or stored within the workcenter and procedures/processes involving them. 

Order all potentially hazardous materials through the Hazmat Pharmacy. 
Identify all operations, including non-routine tasks, involving hazardous chemicals.

Ensure supervisor and worker hazardous materials training are accomplished. 

Request technical training assistance from Public Health Flight, as deemed necessary.

selectedModules.title: Bloodborne Pathogens
selectedModules.reference: 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide bloodborne pathogens training at initial assignment and at least annually thereafter, covering exposure control, modes of transmission, and protective measures.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Enroll applicable workers in the local bloodborne pathogens program and ensure exposure control plan requirements, reporting actions, and PPE procedures are covered before task performance.
selectedModules.notes:
Reference: DPW OMD Safety Program, 29 CFR 1910.1030 
OSHA STD 29 CFR 1910.1030 defines bloodborne pathogens as pathogenic    microorganisms that are present in human blood and can cause disease in humans. These pathogens include, but are not limited to, hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).  

Occupational Exposure means reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials that may result from the performance of an employee's duties. 

Other Potentially Infectious Materials means (1) The following human body fluids: semen, vaginal secretions, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, pleural fluid, pericardial fluid, peritoneal fluid, amniotic fluid, saliva in dental procedures, any body fluid that is visibly contaminated with blood, and all body fluids in situations where it is difficult or impossible to differentiate between body fluids; (2) Any unfixed tissue or organ (other than intact skin) from a human (living or dead); and (3) HIV-containing cell or tissue cultures, organ cultures, and HIV- or HBV-containing culture medium or other solutions; and blood, organs, or other tissues from experimental animals infected with HIV or HBV. 

Source Individual means any individual, living or dead, whose blood or other potentially infectious materials may be a source of occupational exposure to the employee. Examples include, but are not limited to, hospital and clinic patients; clients in institutions for the developmentally disabled; trauma victims; clients of drug and alcohol treatment facilities; residents of hospices and nursing homes; human remains; and individuals who donate or sell blood or blood components. 

All individuals will report to first line supervisor if possible contact with any bloodborne pathogen has been made. Once reported will immediately report to closest medical treatment facility for evaluation.

selectedModules.title: Hearing Conservation
selectedModules.reference: DAFI 48-127; 29 CFR 1910.95 - Occupational noise exposure
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train noise-exposed employees annually on the effects of noise, the purpose of hearing protectors, the advantages and disadvantages of various protectors, and the purpose of audiometric testing.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Ensure workers enrolled in hearing conservation understand noise hazard areas, double-hearing protection requirements, and local follow-up actions tied to occupational health evaluations.
selectedModules.notes:
AFI 48-127, Occupational Noise and Hearing Conservation. 

Hearing protection will be worn whenever noise levels are above 85dB.

An annual audiogram is required for all individuals who work in an environment where noise levels that exceed the Air Force 85dB levels for safe noise environments.  

Hearing protection is required to be worn whenever traveling to the flightline.  Ensure that all personnel know when regular and double hearing protection is required.

selectedModules.title: Confined Space Program
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 23; 29 CFR 1910.146 - Permit-required confined spaces
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train entrants, attendants, supervisors, and rescue personnel so they understand their duties, hazards, signs and symptoms of exposure, communication procedures, and emergency actions before assignment.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide duty-specific training for permit-required confined space roles, including monitor use, atmospheric hazards, entry permits, and rescue responsibilities before personnel participate in entries.
selectedModules.notes:
DPW OMD Safety Program, DAFMAN 91-203, Confined Spaces, and 29 CFR 1910.146. 
IAW DAFMAN 91-203, "Confined Space" means a space that: 

Is large enough and so configured that an employee can bodily enter and perform assigned work. NOTE: "Entry" means the action by which a person passes through an opening into a permit-required confined space.  Entry includes ensuing work activities in that space and is considered to have occurred as soon as any part of the entrant's body breaks the plane of an opening into the space. 

Has limited or restricted means for entry or exit (for example tanks, vessels, silos, storage bins, hoppers, vaults, and pits are spaces that may have limited means of entry) 

And is not designed for continuous employee occupancy. 


Personnel must NEVER enter a confined space unless trained to do so.  THIS INCLUDES RESCUE; call 911, do not attempt to rescue someone as you will likely end up as a casualty!

selectedModules.title: Manual and Powered Hoists
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 35
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide task-specific training on safe use, load limits, inspections, and operating procedures before workers use hoists in material handling operations.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use local lesson plans or manufacturer instructions to cover pre-use inspections, operator limitations, suspended-load controls, and maintenance reporting requirements.

selectedModules.title: Respiratory Protection Program
selectedModules.reference: DAFI 48-137; 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory protection
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train users before respirator use and at least annually on why the respirator is necessary, how improper fit or maintenance can compromise protection, and how to inspect, don, doff, use, and store the respirator.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Document fit testing and occupational health training on AF Form 2767 and ensure wearers understand emergency-use limits, cartridge change-out, cleaning, and medical qualification requirements.
selectedModules.notes: DPW OMD Safety Program, Use AF Form 2767, Occupational Health Training and Protective Equipment Fit Testing (LRA). Reference: AFOSH Standard 48-137, Respiratory Protection Program.

selectedModules.title: Vehicle Mounted Elevated Work Platforms
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 16
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide model-specific training, safe operating procedures, fall protection expectations, and emergency lowering actions before use of elevated work platforms.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use locally approved lesson plans with hands-on demonstration, written testing, and supervisor certification before operators use mobile elevating work platforms.

selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 1
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide CPR and AED training before assignment where required, and refresh qualification before expiration.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Ensure designated responders maintain current certification and understand location and use of local AED assets under the unit mishap prevention program.

selectedModules.title: Flight Line Driving
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 24
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide local flight line driving rules, markings, vehicle lighting requirements, restricted areas, and aircraft hazard awareness before granting driving privileges.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use installation or unit-approved training and certification for airfield/fight line operations, to include local speed, spotter, and no-lone-zone requirements.
selectedModules.afTrainingBasis: DAFMAN 91-203 / Aircraft Flight Line – Ground Operations and Activities
selectedModules.notes: DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 24, Aircraft Flight Line Ground Operations and Activities, and other governing directives.

selectedModules.title: Fetal Protection Program
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 48-146
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide job-specific hazard awareness for reproductive health risks where occupational exposures may affect pregnant workers or fetuses.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use occupational and environmental health guidance to discuss declaration options, exposure review, and local work restriction procedures.
selectedModules.notes: DPW OMD Safety Program, AFI 48-145. Note: Air Force Reserve AFRCI 41-104, Pregnancy of Air Force Reserve Personnel.

selectedModules.title: Electromagnetic Field Training
selectedModules.reference: DAFI 48-109
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Provide task-specific training on electromagnetic field hazards, posting requirements, access controls, and reporting expectations where EMF sources are present.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use approved EMF hazard assessments and local instructions to brief workers on hazard zones, signs, and restrictions before exposure.

selectedModules.title: Ladder Safety
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 7
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers to inspect ladders before use, maintain three points of contact, set ladders on stable surfaces, and avoid overreaching or using damaged ladders.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide hands-on ladder safety training at first assignment, including local storage, damaged-tag procedures, and fall prevention expectations.
selectedModules.notes: DPW OMD Safety Program, DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 7, Walking Surfaces, Guarding Floor and Wall Openings, Fixed Industrial Stairs, and Portable and Fixed Ladders.

selectedModules.title: Active Shooter Response
selectedModules.reference: Installation emergency management guidance / local procedures
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Brief personnel on how to recognize an active shooter event, how to summon help, and how to apply local run-hide-fight guidance based on the facility layout.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use local emergency response procedures, shelter locations, and mass notification methods applicable to the duty location.
selectedModules.notes: Lock down in place at both Exterior (Building 566) and Interior (Building 2045). Barricade entryways and turn off lights while keeping quiet.

selectedModules.title: Government Vehicle / Utility Vehicle Use
selectedModules.reference: DAFI 91-207; local procedures
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train vehicle operators on seat belts, speed limits, local traffic hazards, spotter use while backing, and restrictions on electronic device use while driving.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Brief operators on unit-specific government vehicle training requirements, local route restrictions, low-speed vehicle rules, and documentation of qualification.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Vehicle and Mobile Equipment Concepts

selectedModules.title: Manual Lifting and Material Handling
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards, Chapter 20
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on proper lifting techniques, team lifting, load assessment, and use of lifting aids to reduce musculoskeletal injury risk.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Provide verbal and written guidance on manual lifting, lifting devices, and local reporting actions for strain or overexertion symptoms.
selectedModules.trainingBasis: OSHA 2254 / Ergonomics and Material Handling Concepts

selectedModules.title: Fire Protection and Prevention
selectedModules.reference: DAFMAN 91-203 - Air Force Occupational Safety, Fire and Health Standards; local fire prevention plan
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train personnel on fire hazards, reporting procedures, extinguisher locations, evacuation routes, pull stations, and local emergency response actions.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use the JSTO and local fire prevention plan to brief workers on work-center fire hazards, alarm reporting, extinguisher use, and evacuation accountability.

selectedModules.title: Jewelry / Loose Articles Restrictions
selectedModules.reference: Local procedures / equipment guidance
selectedModules.trainingRequirement: Train workers on removing jewelry and securing loose articles when working around machinery, electrical hazards, rotating equipment, or snag hazards.
selectedModules.afTrainingRequirement: Use local work-center restrictions and equipment guidance to define prohibited items and exceptions for mission-essential tasks.
selectedModules.notes:
DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 9, Jewelry, and applicable technical orders. 

The supervisor should evaluate all jewelry before an individual begins work. Finger rings and jewelry (to include watches) will not be worn by personnel engaged in the following activities or operations: 

Climbing or ascending/descending where the ring (or jewelry) may catch on an object resulting in an injury. 
Performing aircraft maintenance 
Certain materials handling operations. 
Work where workers are exposed to moving machinery. 
Any type of work or inspection where an individual is exposed to electrical circuits.
When working with or around aircraft or vehicle batteries.
